ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
The basic principle of hydroelectric power generation is to convert the mechanical energy of water flow (primarily gravitational potential energy) into electrical energy. A small hydroelectric power station has a water flow rate of $Q = 5\,\mathrm{m}^{3}/\mathrm{s}$ (flow rate refers to the volume of fluid passing through a cross-sectional area per unit time), a head of $h = 10\,\mathrm{m}$, and the generator (with negligible internal resistance) outputs a voltage of $U_{1} = 250\,\mathrm{V}$. The total resistance of the transmission line is $r = 4\,\Omega$. To reduce losses, high-voltage transmission is employed. A step-up transformer is installed at the generator, and a step-down transformer is installed at the user end, with a turns ratio of $n_{3}:n_{4} = 190:11$. The user receives a voltage of $U_{4} = 220\,\mathrm{V}$ and a power of $P_{4} = 1.9 \times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{W}$. Assuming no energy loss in the transformers, the density of water is $\rho = 1.0 \times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{kg}/\mathrm{m}^{3}$, and the acceleration due to gravity is $g = 10\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$.

1. The current intensity in high-voltage transmission lines $I_{2}$
2. The turns ratio of the primary and secondary coils of a step-up transformer is $n_{1}:n_{2}$.
3. What is the efficiency $\eta$ of converting water energy into electrical energy at this power station?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached circuit diagram shows an AC generator/source on the left feeding a step-up transformer. Its primary coil is labeled n1 with voltage U1, and its secondary coil is labeled n2 with voltage U2. The secondary side feeds a long transmission line; the line contains a total resistance r marked on the lower wire. At the receiving end, the line enters the primary coil n3 of a step-down transformer with voltage U3. The secondary coil n4 has voltage U4 and supplies the electrical appliance on the right. Reasoning: The user-side appliance current is I4 = P4 / U4 = 1.9×10^5 W / 220 V = 9500/11 A. For the ideal step-down transformer, U3/U4 = n3/n4 = 190/11, so U3 = 220×190/11 = 3800 V. Also for an ideal transformer, I3/I4 = n4/n3 = 11/190, so I3 = (9500/11)×(11/190) = 50 A. This is the same as the high-voltage transmission line current, so I2 = 50 A. The voltage drop on the line is I2 r = 50×4 = 200 V. Therefore the sending-end high-voltage side of the step-up transformer must be U2 = U3 + I2 r = 3800 + 200 = 4000 V. For the ideal step-up transformer, n1/n2 = U1/U2 = 250/4000 = 1/16, so n1:n2 = 1:16. The generator electrical output sent into the step-up transformer is P2 = U2 I2 = 4000×50 = 2.0×10^5 W. The hydraulic input power is Pwater = ρgQh = 1000×10×5×10 = 5.0×10^5 W. Hence the conversion efficiency is η = P2/Pwater = 2.0×10^5 / 5.0×10^5 = 0.40 = 40%. Final answer: I2 = 50 A; n1:n2 = 1:16; η = 40%.
